summary: W123 "Unknown command" false-positives (plus a harmful quick-fix) on bare `exists`/`get` calls inside a proc defined in the ::tcl::dict namespace, which legitimately resolve via ordinary namespace-relative lookup to the real builtin commands ::tcl::dict::exists / ::tcl::dict::get. Separately, the W001 diagnostic for `dict getnull` at the call site is also a false positive, and it is internally inconsistent with the LSP's own hover/go-to-definition, which correctly resolve `dict getnull` to ::tcl::dict::getnull.
failure_scenario: tcllib's dicttool.tcl (and 4 sibling blocks in the same file: print/is_dict/rmerge/isnull) does `proc ::tcl::dict::getnull {dictionary args} { if {[exists $dictionary {*}$args]} { get $dictionary {*}$args } }` then patches `namespace ensemble configure dict -map` to add "getnull" -> ::tcl::dict::getnull. Reduced to a self-contained 25-line file (dicttool.tcl in the repro dir) and run under tclsh9.0/tclsh8.6: `dict getnull [dict create a 1 b 2] a` correctly prints `1`, and `info commands ::tcl::dict::*` proves ::tcl::dict::exists and ::tcl::dict::get are genuine, pre-existing builtin commands (they back the dict-ensemble's own exists/get subcommands), reachable by bare name from any proc lexically defined inside ::tcl::dict via standard current-namespace-then-global resolution. The LSP instead reports: `HINT W123 9:9-9:15 Unknown command 'exists'; did you mean 'exit'?` and `HINT W123 10:6-10:9 Unknown command 'get'; did you mean 'gets'?`, and hover/go-to-definition on those same tokens return nothing. Worse, `code-actions` at 9:9-9:15 offers a [quickfix] "Replace with 'exit'" — applying it would silently turn `if {[exists $dictionary {*}$args]} {...}` into `if {[exit $dictionary {*}$args]} {...}`, which terminates the process instead of testing dict membership. A control test (`namespace eval ::foo {proc helper {} {...}}; proc ::foo::bar {} {helper}`) shows ordinary user-namespace bare-name resolution works fine with zero diagnostics, and a control with `::tcl::dict::exists`/`::tcl::dict::get` called fully-qualified also produces zero diagnostics — so the gap is specifically: bare-name resolution against registry-known ensemble-subcommand implementation targets (::tcl::dict::*) when the call site is lexically inside that same core namespace. Separately, `dict getnull $clay a` at the call site is flagged `WARNING W001 20:19-20:26 Unknown subcommand 'getnull' for 'dict'` even though hover/definition on the identical token correctly resolve to `proc ::tcl::dict::getnull` at 8:7-8:27 — the diagnostics pass and the hover/definition pass disagree with each other on the same file/token, which is a self-inconsistency independent of whether simulating the `namespace ensemble configure -map` patch is considered in-scope.
root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/unresolved.rs, Analyser::emit_unresolved_command_diagnostics (W123). Its documented resolution order (registry_names / proc_tail_names / class_tail_names / alias_names / rename_target_names / ensemble_cmds / import_pattern_tails) has no path for "bare name relative to the enclosing lexical namespace, matched against a registry command whose full name is <enclosing-namespace>::<name>". rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/dict.rs registers "exists"/"get" purely as ensemble subcommand specs of "dict" (name: "exists", name: "get"), never as standalone commands reachable at ::tcl::dict::exists / ::tcl::dict::get, so W123's registry_names lookup (a flat/global set) can't see them when referenced bare from inside a proc whose namespace is ::tcl::dict. Separately, the W001 "unknown subcommand for ensemble" check (likely in the same diagnostics module or analyser/commands.rs) evidently consults a different/static ensemble-map view than the one the definition/hover resolver (rust/tcl-lsp-core or analyser/scope.rs) uses, since the latter successfully resolves `dict getnull` to ::tcl::dict::getnull by proc-name convention while the former does not — worth checking whether unifying them on the same "known ensemble targets" set is straightforward.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs, `lookup_var_in_scope_chain` (~line 773-825). The `if !name.contains("::") && ... ScopeKind::Namespace` branch (line 794) is the only path that does correct namespace-frame variable lookup, and it's explicitly gated to skip whenever `name` contains `::`. For a qualified name the function falls through to the generic "walk outward, `sc.variables.get(name)`" loop (lines 814-823), which looks for a variable literally keyed by the full qualified string (e.g. "::simple::v") in each scope on the *cursor's* lexical chain — but VarDef entries are stored under their bare/local name inside the scope that owns them (e.g. the `::simple` namespace scope's `variables` map has key "v"), so a `::`-qualified name can never match there. This function is the single shared resolver reused by `hover.rs:182`, `definition.rs:134`, `references.rs:298`/`1276`, `rename.rs:193`/`210`/`657`/`668`, and `completion.rs:1057` — so the gap silently disables hover/definition/references/rename for every fully-qualified variable reference in the codebase, not just the uri.tcl register/namespace-current pattern. A fix needs to split a qualified `name` into (namespace-path, local-name), resolve/walk to the scope matching that namespace path (handling `::`-absolute vs relative-to-cursor's-namespace forms, and the `[namespace current]`/`[namespace parent ...]` command-substitution folding used throughout uri.tcl, which presumably happens upstream in the analyser before this function sees the string).

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:2271-2299 `handle_rename` — the `if crate::naming::is_dynamic_word(&args[0]) || crate::naming::is_dynamic_word(&args[1]) { return true; }` guard at line 2275-2277 gives up on any `$`/`[`-containing rename argument instead of first trying to fold it via the same machinery `resolve_const_word`/`lookup_const_string` (handlers.rs:424-444) already provide for other hooks (e.g. resolve_expansion_count's "var with const value" case, handlers.rs test at line 5097). Fixing would mean: for each of args[0]/args[1], if it's a single Var token (or, for the tcllib idiom, a concatenation of literal text + a resolvable-constant Var), resolve it via lookup_const_string in the current scope before falling back to "dynamic"; only truly non-constant substitutions should hit the early return. naming::is_dynamic_word itself (rust/tcl-syntax/src/naming.rs:891-893) is a pure lexical check with no scope/const-value awareness, so any caller relying on it alone will have the same blind spot.

summary: The analyser's W123 "unknown command" suppression for a per-namespace `namespace unknown` handler only fires when the source contains a literal top-level `namespace unknown ...` invocation. It misses the extremely common tcllib idiom `namespace eval $ns [list namespace unknown $handler]` (verbatim from the mined file, tcllib's modules/namespacex/namespacex.tcl:157-162, `hook::Set`), where "namespace"/"unknown" are only data words fed to `list`, never a real command node. Result: a false-positive W123 "Unknown command" hint on a call that provably resolves correctly at runtime under both tclsh8.6 and tclsh9.0.
failure_scenario: Repro at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-tcl-lsp/b4c77bf3-47fd-5ba4-822a-000fa233bcc1/scratchpad/audit/110/repro.tcl: a `::hooklib` library (a faithful, self-contained extraction of namespacex.tcl's hook::add/Get/Set/Handle) installs a per-namespace `namespace unknown` handler for `::target` via `Set $ns handler` where `Set` does `namespace eval $ns [list namespace unknown $handler]`. `::target::run` then calls the bareword `mystery arg1 arg2`, which is not defined anywhere in the file. Ground truth (tclsh9.0 and tclsh8.6): `mystery` resolves through the installed handler chain and prints `handled:mystery arg1 arg2`, exit code 0 -- no error. LSP diagnostics on the identical file report `HINT W123 67:16-67:23 Unknown command 'mystery'` (0-based line 67 / col 16-23 == exactly the token "mystery", verified byte-for-byte with a Python slice). A minimal-diff control (control_direct.tcl) that installs the *same* handler via the literal form `namespace unknown [namespace code fallbackHandler]` (no `list`/`namespace eval` indirection) produces 0 diagnostics -- correct suppression -- proving the gap is specifically the `list`-wrapped/`namespace eval`-indirected installation idiom, not `namespace unknown` support in general. summary: Mined pattern: docstrip_util.tcl:70-76 does `set c [interp create -safe]; $c eval {proc unknown args {}}; $c alias pkgProvide [namespace which PkgProvide]` — creating a named/handle-returning child interpreter and then dispatching into it via the interpreter's own object command (`$c eval {...}`), the standard real-world idiom. Building a minimal, faithful, literal-name repro of this exposed two distinct, deterministic, statically-resolvable bugs in the analyser, both rooted in how `interp create` is modelled: (1) `interp create -safe NAME` (or `interp create -- NAME`) never registers NAME as a known command, so every later literal call to it raises a false W123 "Unknown command" diagnostic on perfectly valid code — root cause: `record_registry_defined_command` (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs ~2205-2231) reads the interp `create` subcommand's `defines_command_at: Some(0)` (rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/interp.rs ~133) as a fixed index into the raw sub-args without skipping the leading `-safe`/`--` option words first, so it lands on the flag token, sees it starts with '-', and bails out with nothing recorded (`interp create NAME` with no flag works fine, confirming the flag-skip is the missing piece — the interp.rs doc comment even says the flags are "consumed by the leading-option skip" but no such skip exists in the generic consumer). (2) Because `NAME eval {...}` / `$handle eval {...}` (the interpreter object command's own `eval` subcommand) is only recognised as a child-interpreter-isolated body when spelled as literal `interp eval NAME {...}` (handle_interp_eval_command in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs, dispatched only off the literal `interp` command word), the far more common `NAME eval {...}` idiom is never isolated, walked, or scoped at all — no symbols are produced for procs defined inside it. Hover/go-to-definition on a call inside that unscoped block then falls back to a scope-blind, file-wide "any proc anywhere with this bare name" match: with two separate safe child interpreters (sandboxA via literal `interp eval`, sandboxB via the `NAME eval {...}` idiom) each independently defining their own `proc helper`/`proc main`, a call to `helper` inside sandboxB's own script incorrectly resolves (both `definition` and `hover`) to sandboxA's unrelated `helper`, i.e. the wrong interpreter's proc entirely — a genuinely different program point at runtime, not merely an imprecise answer. When no colliding name exists elsewhere in the file, the same call correctly returns 0 locations (proving it's specifically a same-name collision across interpreter boundaries, not partial support), and `references` on sandboxA's `helper` correctly excludes sandboxB's call, showing the incoherence is specifically in the definition/hover fallback path.

summary: The analyser's cross-domain `interp alias` tracking (added for issue #945 fault 8) only fires when the child interpreter's path is a literal token; it silently never fires for `set mpip [interp create -safe]` — the idiom doctools.tcl actually uses at line 692 and that virtually all real Tcl safe-interp code uses (since `interp create` without an explicit name auto-generates one). This causes the LSP to emit a false-positive "Unknown command" (W123) diagnostic and to miss go-to-definition for a command that is genuinely, statically resolvable via the alias.
failure_scenario: doctools.tcl:692-704 does `set mpip [interp create -safe]` then `interp alias $mpip dt_source {} ::doctools::Source $mpip [file dirname $format]` (and similarly for `file`, `dt_read`, `dt_package`), then sources plugin files into `$mpip`; those plugin files call bareword `dt_source`/`file`, which actually resolve to `::doctools::Source`/`::doctools::FileOp` in the master interp via the alias. Minimal repro isolates this: `b/main.tcl` = `namespace eval ::app {}` / `proc ::app::Helper {} { return 42 }` / `set s [interp create -safe]` / `interp alias $s greet {} ::app::Helper` / `interp eval $s { greet }`. tclsh9.0 ground truth: this prints 42 when the return value is captured — the alias unambiguously resolves. A byte-for-byte control that only changes the interp path from a variable to a literal (`a/main.tcl`: `interp create -safe s` / `interp alias s greet {} ::app::Helper` / `interp eval s { greet }`) produces 0 diagnostics and a correct `definition` hit on `::app::Helper` (`main.tcl 2:5-2:18`) — proving the LSP *can* do this resolution, it just never fires when the interp handle is variable-held. root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs: `handle_interp_create_command` (~line 1232) returns early with nothing recorded when `interp create` gets no explicit literal path ("A missing path auto-generates a name this file cannot reference literally, so nothing is recorded"). summary: Hover/go-to-definition/find-references all fail to resolve any fully-qualified namespace variable reference ($::ns::var or $ns::var), even though the reference is 100% statically resolvable (literal namespace, literal variable name, single unambiguous declaration) — reproduced verbatim on tcllib's defer.tcl at the `$::defer::idVar` sentinel used by the trace-based scope-exit mechanism.
failure_scenario: tcllib's modules/defer/defer.tcl declares `variable idVar "<defer>\n<trace variable>"` inside `namespace eval ::defer { ... }` (line 28), then references it via the fully-qualified form `$::defer::idVar` at 3 sites: `with` (line 89, registers the unset-trace whose callback body is the dynamically-built apply-lambda string), and `cancel` (lines 106 and 114, reads/removes trace entries via `trace info variable $::defer::idVar` / `trace remove variable $::defer::idVar ...`). This is the one part of the whole defer/apply/string-match mechanism that IS fully static — a plain namespace-eval variable declaration, referenced by its unambiguous fully-qualified name, no computed names anywhere. Running `python3 lsp_client.py definition defer.tcl 88 46` (0-based line/col landing exactly on `idVar` in `$::defer::idVar` at the real tcllib file's line 89 `trace add variable` call) returns `Definition (0 locations)`; `hover defer.tcl 88 46` returns `(no hover)`; `references defer.tcl 27 10` (cursor on the `idVar` token of the declaration itself, line 28) returns `References (0 locations)`. Ground truth: the LSP's own `symbols` output for this same file independently lists `Namespace ::defer (line 25) / Variable idVar (line 28)`, i.e. the analyser's own symbol index has already identified this exact declaration as the variable's home — hover/definition/references just never reach it. Isolated minimal control (outside defer.tcl) confirms this is a general, not defer-specific, gap: `namespace eval ::foo { variable bar "hi" }` + `proc ::foo::show {} { puts $::foo::bar }` also gives 0 definitions / no hover on `$::foo::bar`, and the same fails for the non-double-colon-rooted `$foo::bar` form too. By contrast, a positive control using the ordinary `variable bar; puts $bar` (local alias) idiom in the same file DOES resolve correctly (`definition` returns the `variable bar` declaration line, `hover` shows `**Variable** bar / 1 reference(s)`) — proving the harness/methodology is sound and isolating the defect to qualified-name (`::ns::var`) resolution specifically. Root cause: `lookup_var_in_scope_chain` in rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/definition.rs (~line 773) takes the raw cursor-extracted name (which correctly includes the "::" segments — `find_var_at_position`'s `scan_var_name_end` in rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs line ~102 explicitly handles "::" as part of a variable name) and, whenever that name contains "::", falls straight into a scope-chain walk doing `sc.variables.get(name)` with the full qualified string as the literal map key. But `define_var` in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/scope.rs (~line 772-821) always inserts into `scope.variables` under the *base* (unqualified) name only (`base_owned = normalise_var_name(name)` — e.g. "idVar", never "::defer::idVar"); the fully-qualified key only exists in the separate `result.all_variables` map, which rust/tcl-lsp-core never reads (`grep -rn all_variables rust/tcl-lsp-core/src` finds zero hits). So `sc.variables.get("::defer::idVar")` can never succeed for any scope, on any file — the qualified-name lookup path is dead code that always returns None. Interestingly the LSP already has the inverse machinery (`qualified_var_name` / `cross_namespace_qualified_vars` in the same file, used by completion) that builds `::ns::var` strings from a scope+base-name pair for autocomplete suggestions, but nothing splits an already-typed qualified name back into (namespace scope, base name) to do the reverse lookup for hover/definition/references.

summary: irc.tcl's own dispatch mechanic (eval $dispatch($linedata(action)), a runtime-keyed/runtime-valued table populated via cmd-registerevent) is correctly and appropriately abstained on by the LSP -- no false resolutions, sensible W101/W307 warnings, matching tclsh ground truth. But probing the surrounding mechanic that produces that dispatch table -- irc.tcl's per-connection dynamic namespace idiom (`set name [format ...]; namespace eval $name { ...many procs... }`, i.e. the exact "irc$conn::$host" pattern called out in the note) -- turned up a real, deterministic bug: handle_namespace_eval_command keys the child scope purely on the raw source text of the (non-literal) namespace-name argument, with no per-call-site disambiguation. Two textually-independent `namespace eval $name { ... }` blocks that happen to use the same variable name (e.g. both named `name`, an extremely common choice for exactly this idiom) get their proc definitions collapsed into one qualified-name key, so go-to-definition/find-references from one instance's call site resolve to a completely unrelated proc defined in the other instance.
failure_scenario: Minimal repro (collision_ws/collision.tcl): two independent factories `::irc::makeA` and `::irc::makeB`, each of the classic irc.tcl per-instance shape `set name [format ...]; namespace eval $name { proc helper {} {...}; proc callHelper {} { helper } }`, both using the local variable name `name`. At runtime (tclsh9.0 and tclsh8.6 agree) these are two fully independent namespaces: `${a}::callHelper` returns "A-helper", `${b}::callHelper` returns "B-helper" -- `helper` inside A's block can ONLY ever bind to A's own `helper` (Tcl's lexical/namespace command resolution guarantees this regardless of what `$name`'s runtime value is). Go-to-definition on the `helper` call inside A's `callHelper` (line 20, col 20, 0-based) should land on A's `proc helper` at line 16 (0-based 15:13-15:19). Instead the LSP returns a single wrong location: `collision.tcl 30:13-30:19` -- B's `helper` definition -- for BOTH A's and B's call sites (identical wrong answer from either query, reproduced twice for determinism). find-references from A's own definition site likewise omits A's definition and instead returns B's definition plus both call sites, i.e. the two independent symbols are silently merged into one. Control test (variant.tcl, same code but variables renamed `nameA`/`nameB`) shows the collision disappears and definition correctly resolves to A's own `proc helper` -- pinning the root cause to the raw-text keying of the dynamic namespace-name argument. Also observed as a real cross-file instance: opening the actual tcllib modules/irc/irc.tcl (copied to real_irc.tcl) alongside my other repro files (which reuse `::irc` + variable name `name`) in the same workspace caused references on irc.tcl's own `cmd-log` proc to pull in unrelated procs from the other files.
root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:1025-1065, `handle_namespace_eval_command` -- line 1034 `let ns_name = args[1].clone();` uses the raw (unresolved, non-literal) source text of the `namespace eval` target argument directly as the new child Scope's name, with no per-call-site uniqueification (contrast with the `interp eval` handler right below it at handlers.rs:1086+, which explicitly notes "a dynamic path ($i) can't collide with a real namespace, so it stays conservatively isolated" and mints a synthetic `@interp@<path>` domain). Downstream, this qualified-name text is used as the key into a flat `pub all_procs: HashMap<String, ProcDef>` (rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/types.rs:773), so a second `namespace eval $name { ... }` block whose target variable happens to share the same literal name silently overwrites/merges the first block's proc entries. Fix direction: when the namespace-eval argument is non-literal, mint a synthetic per-call-site scope name (e.g. incorporating source span or a counter) instead of reusing the raw variable-reference text, mirroring the `@interp@<path>` treatment already used for `interp eval`.

summary: clay.tcl's `Ensemble` DSL (custom oo::define keyword that synthesizes a method name via string ops and installs it with `oo::define $class method $realmethod ...`) is correctly abstained-on by hover/definition/diagnostics (no false positives, no crash). But textDocument/documentSymbol has a genuine, deterministic bug: handle_oo_define_command merges ClassDef state across unrelated procs whenever they use the same *variable name* (e.g. `$class`) as the oo::define target, because it keys a global class table by the raw (unresolved) argument text instead of scoping per-occurrence. This produces document symbols where a child method's range lies textually outside its claimed parent function's range — a self-contradictory, checkable-from-source-alone structural error, independent of any dynamic-value ambiguity.
root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs, fn handle_oo_define_command (~lines 2680-2781). It computes `qualified = qualify(ns_for_qualify, raw_class_name)` from `args[0]` (line 2690-2693) without distinguishing a literal class-name token from an unresolved variable reference, then does `self.result.all_classes.remove(&qualified).unwrap_or_else(...)` (lines 2717-2739) to find-or-create the ClassDef -- a lookup in a single global, file-wide map keyed by that raw text. Two textually-unrelated procs that both write `oo::define $class method ...` (an extremely common idiom in this exact DSL family -- clay.tcl's own `current_class`-based helpers all use `set class [current_class]`) collide on the same placeholder key, so the second occurrence's handling reads back and extends the first occurrence's ClassDef (methods included), then re-inserts the merged object into *both* the global map and the current call site's `scope.classes` (lines 2774-2779). The per-scope insert at line 2778 is what leaks the unrelated, earlier-discovered method into the later proc's document-symbol subtree, producing a child whose source range sits outside the parent's range. Fix direction: don't merge/key ClassDef state across occurrences when raw_class_name is not a literal (only a `$var`/non-identifier token) -- either skip registration into any scope's `classes` map for unresolved-name oo::define targets, or key by (scope_path, raw_text) rather than raw_text alone so unrelated scopes never share a synthesized ClassDef.

summary: The LSP's dead-store/unused-variable diagnostic (W220) misreads a variable reference wrapped in unescaped braces (`{$var}`) inside a double-quoted string argument as a non-substituting brace-quoted word, silently dropping it from the SSA "used" set and emitting a false-positive "Assignment to '<var>' is never read" hint — even though the LSP's own hover/definition/references engine correctly resolves that exact same `$var` occurrence as a live read.
failure_scenario: Real pattern (tcllib modules/htmlparse/htmlparse.tcl:792-893, proc ::htmlparse::parse): `set vroot hmstart` followed later by `eval "$cmd {$vroot} {} {} \{$html\}"`. Braces have no word-grouping meaning inside an already-open double-quoted string (only `$`, `[`, `\`, and the closing `"` are special there), so `{$vroot}` is an ordinary substitution of `vroot`, exactly like the bare `$cmd` and the backslash-escaped `\{$html\}` beside it. Ground truth (tclsh9.0/8.6) confirms all three are read: running the minimal repro prints "default callback: hmstart {} {} <b>hi</b>" — `vroot`'s value ("hmstart") is clearly consumed. Yet `diagnostics` on the repro reports `HINT W220 30:8-30:13 Assignment to 'vroot' is never read`, while `$cmd` and `$html` (assigned the same way, read the same way) are correctly NOT flagged. Isolated further (general_test.tcl: `set s "prefix {$a} suffix"` with no eval at all) reproduces the identical false positive, proving the bug lives in the shared brace/quote re-lexing of extracted word text, not in eval-specific handling. Internal inconsistency proof: `references`/`definition`/`hover` invoked on the exact same `$vroot`/`$a` token inside the eval string correctly return the `set` statement as a reference/definition (2-3 locations including the def), directly contradicting the "never read" diagnostic computed from the same source.
root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_refs.rs `VarReferenceScanner::scan_script_uncached` re-tokenizes already-extracted argument/value text with the general-purpose `tcl_lexer::Lexer`, which applies top-level command-word rules (bare `{...}` = brace-quoted, unsubstituted word) to text that actually originated *inside* a double-quoted string, where braces are ordinary characters and substitution continues through them. Callers that feed raw AssignValue/Call-arg text into `scan_word` — rust/tcl-compiler/src/ssa.rs (e.g. the AssignValue-uses helper around line 1291 and the Call-arg-uses helper around line 1466) — inherit this mis-tokenization, so the SSA `used` set omits `vroot`/`a`. That omission flows straight into rust/tcl-compiler/src/dead_stores.rs's `liveness_dead_stores`, producing the false W220 hint. The go-to-definition/references/hover code path does not share this defect (it matches oracle truth), so the fix should make the shared word/value re-scan quote-context-aware — e.g. track whether the text being re-lexed is itself the interior of a double-quoted string (so `{`/`}` must not be treated as word-brace delimiters) — or, more robustly, have the SSA use-computation walk the original CST spans (as the definition/references/hover pass apparently does) instead of re-lexing extracted text strings from scratch.

summary: The assigned mechanic itself (::tcl::mathop::* / ::tcl::mathop::+ passed as first-class command-name values into foldl/reduce, invoked via {*}$f) is handled correctly: hover on the literal ::tcl::mathop::* / ::tcl::mathop::+ tokens gives correct builtin docs, go-to-definition correctly abstains (no Tcl source exists for a C builtin), and diagnostics are clean. But testing this pattern's host procs (reduce/foldl, whose params f/z/xs are exactly what carries the mathop value) exposed a real, general, deterministic bug: for any proc with 2+ parameters, only the FIRST parameter gets a correctly resolved declaration span. Every later parameter's definition_span silently falls back to the enclosing proc's own NAME token, so go-to-definition on any use of the 2nd/3rd/... parameter jumps to the proc name instead of the parameter, and find-references for two different later parameters (e.g. z and xs) returns byte-identical, cross-contaminated location sets (each other's references merged, plus the proc-name span spuriously listed as a "declaration").
failure_scenario: Given `proc reduce {f z xs} { foreach x $xs { set z [{*}$f $z $x] }; return $z }` (the real shape backing generator.tcl's foldl/product/sum), running go-to-definition on the `$z` read inside `{*}$f $z $x` returns the span of the token "reduce" (the proc name), not z's own position in `{f z xs}`; the same happens for `$xs`. find-references on z and on xs (different cursor positions, different variables) return the exact same 5 locations for both queries. Only `f` (the first parameter) resolves correctly. Reproduced identically against the real tcllib source at modules/generator/generator.tcl line 188 (`proc reduce {f z xs} {`): go-to-definition on the `$z` at 188:38 and on the `$xs` at 188:19 both return 187:9-187:15 (the "reduce" name span) instead of each parameter's own declaration column; go-to-definition on `$f` at 188:35 correctly returns 187:17-187:18. Also reproduced with a top-level (non-namespaced) 3-param proc and with long descriptive parameter names (func/accum/items) — ruling out namespace-nesting or short-name-length as the cause; it is purely "parameter index >= 1".

The observable merge itself happens downstream in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/definition.rs `linked_var_reference_spans`/`collect_shared_span_refs` (~lines 846-897) and rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/references.rs `variable_references` (~line 286-316): any two VarDefs that end up with an identical `definition_span` (here, both accidentally the proc-name fallback span) are treated as the TclOO-instance-variable aliasing case and their reference lists are unioned — this same code path likely also corrupts Rename (not directly testable via the provided lsp-client subcommands, but references.rs is shared infrastructure with rename.rs).

summary: PackageResolver::parse_pkg_index (rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/package_resolver.rs) scans a pkgIndex.tcl for every top-level `package ifneeded` command and registers it unconditionally, with zero control-flow/reachability modeling of a preceding `if {...} { return }` guard — even a statically-constant `if {1} { return }` that unconditionally exits before it on every Tcl version. This exactly matches the real tcllib idiom in modules/try/pkgIndex.tcl (lines 1-21), where `package ifneeded try/throw/file::home` are top-level statements gated by `package vsatisfies [package provide Tcl] ...` version checks. The W123 (unknown-command) workspace diagnostic refinement trusts this over-permissive package database, so a command that a guarded package can never actually provide under the real interpreter is silently treated as resolvable, suppressing a diagnostic that should fire.
failure_scenario: Workspace: lib/mypkg/pkgIndex.tcl = `if {[package vsatisfies [package provide Tcl] 9-]} { return }\npackage ifneeded mypkg 1.0 [list source [file join $dir mypkg.tcl]]` (faithful shrink of tcllib's file::home gate), lib/mypkg/mypkg.tcl defines `proc mypkgHello {}`. entry.tcl = `package require mypkg` + `source lib_user.tcl`; lib_user.tcl = `mypkgHello`. Under the real Tcl 9.0.4 oracle, the guard's `return` fires, so `package require mypkg` fails ('can't find package mypkg') and calling `mypkgHello` is a genuine 'invalid command name' error — W123 should fire on `mypkgHello` in lib_user.tcl. The LSP instead reports 0 diagnostics for lib_user.tcl (verified stable across 3 repeated runs), because package_resolver.rs's parse_pkg_index registers the trailing top-level `package ifneeded mypkg ...` regardless of the guard, and refine_workspace_w123 (rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs) then treats `mypkgHello` (read from mypkg.tcl) as a legitimate command and suppresses the diagnostic. A clean isolating control confirms the root cause is pure reachability-blindness, not a vsatisfies-parsing quirk: replacing the guard with a trivial, version-independent `if {1} { return }\npackage ifneeded mypkg ...` (unreachable under literally any Tcl version — oracle-confirmed) still yields 0 LSP diagnostics, while nesting the same ifneeded textually *inside* the `if {0} { ... }` block (so it is not even a top-level command) correctly yields the W123 diagnostic. So the bug is specifically: any top-level `package ifneeded` that textually follows an earlier unconditional/guarded early-return is still treated as always-registered.

root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/package_resolver.rs: `parse_pkg_index` (~line 296-342) walks `walk_command_words(content)` and registers any command whose first two words are `package`/`ifneeded`, with no tracking of an enclosing/preceding `if {...} { return }` (or `if {[package vsatisfies ...]} { return }`) that would make the statement unreachable for the running interpreter — it only respects Tcl's own brace grouping (so a `package ifneeded` genuinely nested inside braces, e.g. `if {0} { package ifneeded ... }`, is correctly excluded since it's not a top-level command at all; a sequential top-level statement after an early-return guard is not). Consumed via `PackageResolver::resolve`/`package_defined_commands` (~line 700-831) by `refine_w123_diagnostics`/`refine_workspace_w123` in rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs (~11390-11466), which suppress W123 for any command name found in a "resolvable" package's implementation file. A fix would need either (a) light control-flow modeling in parse_pkg_index — treat an unconditional top-level `return`/`if {<const-true>} { return }` (or, more ambitiously, evaluate `package vsatisfies [package provide Tcl] ...` guards against a configured/detected target Tcl version, mirroring the guard-parsing already done for dialect detection in rust/tcl-registry/src/dialects.rs) as terminating the scan, or (b) treat guarded package registrations as merely 'possibly available' (skip W123 suppression, or downgrade confidence) rather than unconditionally available.

summary: Go-to-definition, references, and diagnostics all correctly resolve a tcllib-style command that is exported from a package-provide file but physically defined only in a sibling file reachable via auto_path/tclIndex (or even a plain `source`) — but hover silently returns nothing at the exact same call-site location, even though the same information is trivially available (the definition provider already found it, and hovering the definition itself, or a same-file call, renders it fine).
failure_scenario: Workspace: main.tcl does `lappend auto_path .../mathlib; package require math; math::zzqfrobnicate 1 2 3 4`. mathlib/math.tcl (mirroring tcllib's modules/math/math.tcl:17-44) only `namespace export`s `zzqfrobnicate`/`wibblenum` and extends `::auto_path`; the real proc bodies live in mathlib/misc.tcl, wired up by mathlib/tclIndex (`set auto_index(::math::zzqfrobnicate) [list source [file join $dir misc.tcl]]`). tclsh9.0 and tclsh8.6 both run this and print `2` / `55` — ground truth confirms `::math::zzqfrobnicate`/`::math::wibblenum` in misc.tcl are the real, unambiguous targets. `lsp_client.py definition main.tcl 3 15` correctly returns `misc.tcl 4:5-4:26` (the exact proc declaration); `references mathlib/misc.tcl 4 17` correctly returns both `misc.tcl 4:5-4:26` and `main.tcl 3:12-3:31`; `diagnostics main.tcl` reports 0 items (no false unknown-command warning). But `lsp_client.py hover main.tcl 3 15` (and every column 12-31 across the same token) returns `(no hover)`, whereas hovering the identical symbol at its own definition site (`hover mathlib/misc.tcl 4 10`) or at a same-file call site (control/onefile.tcl) both render the full `proc ::math::zzqfrobnicate {val args} {...}` signature. A minimal control with a literal `source` instead of auto_path/tclIndex (control2/loader.tcl, control3/loader.tcl with an unqualified global proc) reproduces the identical hover-vs-definition split, showing the gap is a general cross-file hover limitation, not specific to the tclIndex mechanic — but it does affect exactly the assigned tcllib pattern.
root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs: `compute_definition` (~3633-3706) has four resolution tiers — in-document (`core_definition::definition`), cross-file TclOO method (`resolve_method_target`/`cross_file_method_definition`), cross-document workspace-index fallback (`cross_document_definition`), and an explicit "Autoload tier (M8)" (`autoload_definition`, ~3717) that resolves via tclIndex/pkgIndex specifically for this kind of pattern. The `references` handler (~8065) likewise merges local + cross-document hits (see test `references_handler_merges_local_and_cross_document`). By contrast, `hover()` (~9939-9984) calls only `core_hover::hover_with_profile(&doc.text, ..., &analysis, ...)` against the single-document `analysis_for(&uri, ...)` result and never calls `self.cross_document_definition(...)` or `self.autoload_definition(...)` when the in-document lookup misses. rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs's `resolve_called_proc` call (line ~268, reusing `crate::definition::resolve_called_proc`) is likewise only ever given the single-file `AnalysisResult` — there is no cross-file/workspace-index parameter threaded into hover at all, and no test in hover.rs exercises a second file. Fix: in the `hover` handler, when `core_hover::hover_with_profile` returns `None` and the cursor is on a command head, fall back to the same workspace-index / autoload lookup `compute_definition` uses, then format the resulting `ProcDef`/`ClassDef` with the same `proc_hover_text`-style renderer already used for in-document hits.
